title: Callbacks are reactions
description: Let incoming scans update node state, then use a timer to publish a status message. Sensor events and timer events are separate callbacks.
steps: Store the most recent forward distance when a scan arrives.
Use a 0.2-second timer to publish that distance as String on /chatter.
Observe topic hz /scan and topic echo /chatter in separate terminals. Explain which callback updates the state and which publishes it.
hints: Keep front between callbacks. When a function assigns this module variable, write global front before the assignment.
Create the publisher once: publisher = node.create_publisher(String, "/chatter", 10).
Inside the timer callback: status = String(); status.data = str(front); publisher.publish(status).
Register the scan callback with node.create_subscription(LaserScan, "/scan", scan, 10), and the timer with node.create_timer(0.2, tick). rclpy.spin(node) dispatches both callbacks.

content.title: Callbacks are reactions
content.description: Let incoming scans update node state, then use a timer to publish a status message. Sensor events and timer events are separate callbacks.
steps: Store the most recent forward distance when a scan arrives.
Use a 0.2-second timer to publish that distance as String on /chatter.
Observe topic hz /scan and topic echo /chatter in separate terminals. Explain which callback updates the state and which publishes it.
hints: Keep latest_range_ as a node member: the scan callback updates it and the timer reads it.
Create the publisher once: publisher_ = create_publisher<std_msgs::msg::String>("/chatter", 10); retain the subscription and timer handles too.
Inside the timer callback: std_msgs::msg::String status; status.data = std::to_string(latest_range_); publisher_->publish(status);
Register the timer with timer_ = create_wall_timer(std::chrono::milliseconds(200), [this]() { /* publish status here */ });
